```{r}
#| message: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scrutiny)
library(roundwork)
library(strait)
library(analyticgrimu)
```

## Granularity {#sec-granularity-core-idea}

Imagine a study where two participants are asked their age in years, and the article reports "mean age = 23.16". Why is this result impossible?

Ages in years have to be whole numbers (integers), and the mean of two integers must end in either ".00" or ".50". Put another way, the reported mean is inconsistent with the underlying data being integer and the sample size being 2. 

This is the core of granularity methods: The granularity of the underlying data (e.g., integer data from Likert scales) means that summary statistics based on them (e.g., means and standard deviations) also have granularity, where only some numbers are mathematically possible.

Granularity methods are tests of possibility: they ask whether a reported value can exist at all, given what the article says about the data, not whether it is surprising. They need only what is printed: the summary statistics, the sample size, and a description of how the variable was measured. This chapter covers the two most widely used. GRIM (@sec-grim) checks a mean against its sample size, and GRIMMER (@sec-grimmer) adds the SD.

## GRIM: Testing consistency among N/M/integer data {#sec-grim}

The GRIM test (granularity-related inconsistency of means) was introduced by @brown2017. The {scrutiny} package [@jung2026] implements GRIM and the other tests in this chapter.

Use the plot below to see which means can pass GRIM. Each square is a mean as it would be printed to the chosen number of decimals, and the row covers every such mean near the one you enter. The zoom setting chooses how far the row reaches on either side of it: 1 at low zoom, 0.5 at medium, and 0.25 at high. The rounding setting chooses what happens to a mean that falls exactly halfway between two reported values: it may be rounded either up or down, or only up (@nte-grim-rounding). Leave the number of items averaged at 1 unless each participant's score is the mean of several items. A square is black if some set of *N* whole numbers has that mean, and white if no set does. Typing a mean centres the row on it. Clicking or dragging in the row chooses a mean without moving the row. The chosen mean is circled in blue.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof grim1Mean = Inputs.number({label: "Reported mean", value: 23.16, step: 0.01, width: 90})
viewof grim1N = Inputs.range([2, 100], {label: "Sample size (N)", step: 1, value: 2})
viewof grim1Digits = Inputs.select([1, 2], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})
viewof grim1Items = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof grim1Rounding = Inputs.select(new Map([["Up or down", "up_or_down"], ["Half up", "up"]]), {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})
viewof grim1Zoom = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Low", 1], ["Medium", 0.5], ["High", 0.25]]), {label: "Zoom", value: 0.5})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// the centre of the row. it moves to the mean when the mean is typed in, and stays put when the mean is chosen by
// clicking or dragging in the plot, or when anything else changes
grim1View = ({mean: 23.16, recentre: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  // typing fires an input event on the text box itself, whereas clicking in the plot sets the value on the whole input
  viewof grim1Mean.querySelector("input").addEventListener("input", () => { grim1View.recentre = true })
  return html``
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = grim1Digits, scale = 10 ** d, nk = grim1N * grim1Items
  if (!Number.isFinite(grim1Mean) || !Number.isInteger(grim1Items) || grim1Items < 1) return html`<p style="font-weight: 600;">Enter a mean and a whole number of items.</p>`
  const blue = "#2780e3", red = "#c0392b"
  const v = grim1View
  if (v.recentre) Object.assign(v, {mean: grim1Mean, recentre: false})
  // values are handled as whole numbers of reporting steps, so that 5.19 at two decimals is 519. the row reaches the
  // zoom distance (1, 0.5, or 0.25) on either side of its centre, and always at least one reporting step
  const half = Math.max(1, Math.round(grim1Zoom * scale)), size = 2 * half + 1
  const i0 = Math.round(v.mean * scale) - half
  // GRIM: some whole-number sum S has a mean, S / (N x items), that is reported as i / scale. a mean exactly halfway
  // between two reported values may be rounded either way ("up or down"), or only up ("half up"), in which case the
  // top of the interval is excluded
  const halfUp = grim1Rounding === "up"
  const attainable = i => {
    const top = nk * (i + 0.5) / scale
    return Math.ceil(nk * (i - 0.5) / scale - 1e-9) <= (halfUp ? Math.ceil(top - 1e-9) - 1 : Math.floor(top + 1e-9))
  }
  const fills = d3.range(size).map(c => attainable(i0 + c) ? "black" : "white")
  const ix = Math.round(grim1Mean * scale), consistent = attainable(ix)
  // the test is uninformative when every mean that can be printed at this precision passes. only the decimal part of a
  // mean matters, so it is enough to check the endings from 0 to scale - 1. this also catches sample sizes where
  // rounding halves either way makes every value pass before N x items reaches 10^d
  const uninformative = d3.range(scale).every(attainable)
  const verdict = uninformative ? ["GRIM-uninformative", "#6c757d"] : consistent ? ["GRIM-consistent", blue] : ["GRIM-inconsistent", red]
  const who = `${grim1N} participants${grim1Items > 1 ? `, each scored as the average of ${grim1Items} items,` : ""}`
  // the same left margin and width as the plot of means and SDs further down, so that the two line up
  const margins = {marginLeft: 64, marginRight: 10, marginTop: 10, marginBottom: 45}
  const frame = Math.min(520, width - margins.marginLeft - margins.marginRight)
  const plotWidth = frame + margins.marginLeft + margins.marginRight
  const plotHeight = 60 + margins.marginTop + margins.marginBottom
  const xDomain = [(i0 - 0.5) / scale, (i0 + size - 0.5) / scale]
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: plotWidth, height: plotHeight, ...margins,
    x: {label: "Reported mean", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: xDomain, ticks: Math.max(3, Math.floor(frame / 60)), tickFormat: t => t.toFixed(d)},
    y: {axis: null, domain: [0, 1]},
    color: {type: "identity"},
    style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
    marks: [
      Plot.raster(fills, {width: size, height: 1, x1: xDomain[0], x2: xDomain[1], y1: 1, y2: 0, fill: f => f, imageRendering: "pixelated"}),
      Plot.frame({stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
      Plot.dot([{}], {x: ix / scale, y: 0.5, r: 7, fill: "none", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 5}),
      Plot.dot([{}], {x: ix / scale, y: 0.5, r: 7, fill: "none", stroke: blue, strokeWidth: 2.5})
    ]
  })
  // clicking or dragging in the plot sets the mean to the square under the pointer
  clickToSet(plot, {width: plotWidth, height: plotHeight, ...margins, xDomain, yDomain: [0, 1]}, m => {
    setInput(viewof grim1Mean, Math.round(m * scale) / scale)
  })
  const legendSquare = (fill, stroke) => `<svg width="14" height="14" style="vertical-align: -2px;"><rect x="1" y="1" width="12" height="12" fill="${fill}" stroke="${stroke}"/></svg>`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = `<span>${legendSquare("black", "black")} Consistent</span>
    <span>${legendSquare("white", "rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.8)")} Inconsistent</span>
    <span><svg width="16" height="16" style="vertical-align: -3px;"><circle cx="8" cy="8" r="6" fill="none" stroke="${blue}" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg> Reported mean and SD</span>`
  return html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.2rem 0;">A mean of ${(ix / scale).toFixed(d)} from ${who} is <span style="color: ${verdict[1]};">${verdict[0]}</span>.</p>
<p style="margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;">Attainable means are ${(1 / nk).toFixed(4)} apart${nk >= 10 ** d ? `, which is no wider than the ${d}-decimal reporting steps, so no mean can fail` : uninformative ? `. With halves rounded either way, that is close enough for every ${d}-decimal mean to be reached, so no mean can fail` : ""}.</p>
${plot}${legend}`
}
```

Try the default values first. They are the age example from @sec-granularity-core-idea: a mean of 23.16 from 2 participants. The square for 23.16 is white, because the only attainable means nearby are 23.00 and 23.50. Almost every square is white, because only 2 of every 100 two-decimal means can come from 2 participants. Then raise *N* towards 100 and watch the white squares thin out and disappear, as the attainable means crowd together until every two-decimal mean is attainable (@sec-grim-uninformative). Switch to one decimal place and the white squares are gone from *N* = 10 onwards. Finally, try a mean of 3.12 from 8 participants under each rounding setting. The only whole-number sum near 3.12 × 8 = 24.96 is 25, and the exact mean of 25/8 = 3.125 is reported as 3.12 only if halves can be rounded down (@nte-grim-rounding).

### What counts as whole-number (integer) data {#sec-grim-integer-data}

GRIM's central assumption is that each participant contributes a whole number. The practical skill in using it is knowing when that holds, and what the effective sample size is.

**Explicit single items.** One Likert-type question, one count. The number of response options is irrelevant: it makes no difference whether answers run from 0 to 3 or from 1 to 100 [@brown2017].

**Implicit single-item scales.** Many variables are whole numbers without being thought of as scales: age in years, number of children, years of education, number of sessions attended, days in hospital, number of correct trials, cigarettes per day. These are often the best targets in an article, because they appear in baseline tables for every group and nobody expects them to be checked.

**Multi-item scales.** Here the scoring method decides the granularity.

-   A **sum score** across *k* items is still a whole number for each participant. The mean of sum scores moves in steps of 1/*N*, as for a single item.
-   A **mean score** across *k* items can take any multiple of 1/*k* for each participant. The mean of mean scores moves in steps of 1/(*N* × *k*), so the scale behaves like a single item answered by *N* × *k* people. A 10-item scale with 20 participants has the granularity of a single item with 200, and GRIM at two decimals has nothing to say about it.

The "items" in GRIM is therefore easy to misread. It is not the number of items in the scale. It is the number of items averaged to make each participant's score, before the sample mean was taken. That number is 1 for a single question, and for any variable that is already a whole number for each participant, such as age in years. It is also 1 for a sum score, however many items were added up, because each participant's total is a whole number. It is greater than 1 only when each participant's responses were averaged first and the sample mean was then taken over those averages, and it is then the number of items that were averaged. A 20-item questionnaire scored as a sum has 1 item for GRIM, and the same questionnaire scored as a mean has 20.

This number is an input to the test that has to be extracted from the article, and getting it wrong produces false alarms. Brown and Heathers describe making this mistake themselves: what they took for inconsistent means on a single item turned out to be correctly reported means of a multi-item composite. For subscales, the relevant number is the items in the subscale, not in the full questionnaire. In {scrutiny}, it is given through the `items` argument.

```{r}
# impossible for one item answered by 20 people, possible for the mean of a 3-item scale
grim(x = 3.42, n = 20, digits_x = 2, items = 1)
grim(x = 3.42, n = 20, digits_x = 2, items = 3)
```

**Data that look like whole numbers but are not.** Age calculated from date of birth, response scales that allow half points, visual analogue scales, reaction times, body mass index, and any score that has been weighted, standardised, transformed, or imputed. A scale with half-point options behaves like a two-item scale [@brown2017], and can be tested as one. The others cannot be tested.

**Statistics that GRIM cannot test at all.** Adjusted means, estimated marginal means, conditional means or predicted values from a regression or mixed model, and other model-based estimates are not simple averages of the observed scores, even when the scores are whole numbers.

**Percentages.** A percentage is a mean of zeros and ones multiplied by 100, so GRIM applies to it directly, with *k* = 1. A percentage reported to *d* decimals is a proportion reported to *d* + 2 decimals, so a percentage given to one decimal is testable for samples of up to 999 [@brown2017]. For example, 37.5% of 13 participants is impossible: 4 of 13 is 30.8% and 5 of 13 is 38.5%.

**Missing responses within a scale.** If some participants skipped some items, the number of responses behind a mean score is smaller than *N* × *k*, and the test's grid is wrong. Brown and Heathers found this caused an inconsistency in only one of the articles they examined, partly because multi-item scales are rarely GRIM-testable in the first place.

@tbl-granularity summarises the common cases, including the sample size from which GRIM can no longer fail (@sec-grim-uninformative).

| Measure | Step size of the mean | GRIM at two decimals is uninformative from |
|-------------------------|------------------|-----------------------------|
| Single item, count, or age in years | 1/*N* | *N* = 100 |
| Sum score of *k* items | 1/*N* | *N* = 100 |
| Single item with half-point options | 1/(2*N*) | *N* = 50 |
| Mean score of 3 items | 1/(3*N*) | *N* = 34 |
| Mean score of 5 items | 1/(5*N*) | *N* = 20 |
| Mean score of 10 items | 1/(10*N*) | *N* = 10 |
| Percentage reported to one decimal | 100/*N* | *N* = 1,000 |
| Percentage reported as a whole number | 100/*N* | *N* = 100 |

: Granularity of common measures. {#tbl-granularity}

::: {#nte-grim-rounding .callout-note collapse="true"}
## Rounding

The last example in @sec-grim-grimmer-plot, a mean of 3.12 from 8 participants, has no single answer. Its only candidate sum gives an exact mean of 25/8 = 3.125, which is reported as 3.13 by some software and 3.12 by other software. Rounding gets its own note because, once extraction errors are set aside, it is the main way that a correct value can be flagged as impossible.

#### Rounding conventions

Several conventions are in use for a value that falls exactly halfway between two reportable numbers.

-   **Round half up** (strictly, away from zero): 3.125 becomes 3.13. This is what most people were taught at school, and what SPSS and Excel do.
-   **Round half to even**: 3.125 becomes 3.12 and 3.135 becomes 3.14. This is the default in R and Python.
-   **Round half down**: 3.125 becomes 3.12. Rare as a deliberate choice, but it happens by accident, as described next.
-   **Floating-point artefacts.** Computers store most decimal numbers approximately. A number that looks like an exact half may be stored as very slightly less, and is then rounded down whatever the rule.

```{r}
round(0.125, 2)  # an exact half in binary: rounded to the even digit
round(0.375, 2)  # an exact half in binary: rounded to the even digit
round(2.675, 2)  # stored as 2.67499999..., so rounded down
```

Two further practices are not conventions for halves but change the reported value more broadly.

-   **Truncation**: the extra decimals are cut off, so 3.458 is reported as 3.45. A reported 3.45 could then stand for anything from 3.450 up to just under 3.460. This happens when values are copied by hand from output, or when numbers are formatted as text.
-   **Stepped rounding**: a value is rounded once to an intermediate number of decimals and then again. Brown and Heathers found a real case when they obtained the data behind a set of inconsistent SDs: SPSS had displayed 1.2849 at its default three decimals as 1.285, and the authors had then rounded this by hand to 1.29. The correct two-decimal value is 1.28. Stepped rounding can move a value a full unit in the last decimal place, even when the original was not close to a half.

#### Rounding is an assumption of the test

Authors almost never say how they rounded. They may not know, and different parts of the same article may have been produced by different software. The rounding rule is therefore not a fact about the article that we can look up. It is an assumption that we bring to the test.

The conservative response is to count a value as consistent if *any* reasonable rounding of halves reproduces it. This is what @brown2017 did, and it is the default in {scrutiny} (`rounding = "up_or_down"`). The strict alternatives are available for comparison:

```{r}
grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "up_or_down")
grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "up")
grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "even")
```

Truncation can be allowed for in the same spirit, by also accepting any sum whose mean would be cut down to the reported value. Stepped rounding is harder. {scrutiny} does not accommodate it, and neither does any other GRIM implementation we know of. It should be kept in mind as a possible innocent explanation for a failure, particularly when the reported value is one unit above an attainable one. It is also an undisclosed and incorrect practice, so "the authors rounded twice" is still a finding about the article's reporting, if a minor one.

The practical advice is to run the lenient test as the main analysis, because a false accusation of impossibility is the costlier error, and to report how the verdicts change under stricter rules. A value that only passes because a half was rounded down, in an article whose other values were rounded up, deserves a note.

The rounding of reported values also matters when they are used as *inputs* to other calculations, such as recomputing a *p*-value from rounded means and SDs. That is covered in @sec-recalculation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths: GRIM

Stated formally: a mean reported to *d* decimals is GRIM-consistent if there is a whole-number sum *S* such that *S* / (*N* × items), rounded to *d* decimals, equals the reported mean. Here "items" means the number of items averaged to make each participant's score before the sample mean was taken, not the number of items in the questionnaire. It is 1 for a single question, a whole-number variable such as age in years, and a sum score.

**Without rounding**

Let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be the scores of $N$ participants on a single item, each a whole number. Their sum is a whole number,

$$S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \in \mathbb{Z},$$

and the mean is that sum divided by the sample size,

$$M = \frac{S}{N}.$$

So the exact mean must satisfy

$$N \times M \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

This is the whole of GRIM when the mean is known exactly: multiply the mean by the sample size and check that the result is a whole number. The attainable means form an evenly spaced grid,

$$\mathcal{G}_N = \left\{ \frac{S}{N} : S \in \mathbb{Z} \right\},$$

and the spacing of the grid, $1/N$, is the granularity of the mean.

For a mean score across $k$ items, each participant's score is the mean of $k$ whole numbers, $y_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} x_{ij}$. The sum of all $N \times k$ responses is a whole number, so

$$M = \frac{S}{N k}, \qquad N k \times M \in \mathbb{Z},$$

and the granularity is $1/(Nk)$. A $k$-item mean score from $N$ participants has the same grid as a single item from $Nk$ participants. A sum score across $k$ items is a whole number for each participant, so it is the single-item case.

The minimum and maximum of the response scale appear nowhere in these expressions. They restrict the range of $S$, to between $N k \times \min$ and $N k \times \max$, but not the spacing of the grid.

**With rounding**

Articles report the mean rounded to $d$ decimals. Call the reported value $\tilde{M}$, and let

$$\delta = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{-d}$$

be half of one reporting step, so $\delta = 0.005$ at two decimals. The reported value does not identify the exact mean. It identifies an interval $I(\tilde{M})$ of exact values that would all have been reported as $\tilde{M}$. Which interval depends on the rounding practice (@nte-grim-rounding).

| Rounding practice | Interval of exact means, $I(\tilde{M})$ |
|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Halves rounded up | $[\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta)$ |
| Halves rounded down | $(\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta]$ |
| Halves rounded either way (lenient) | $[\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta]$ |
| Truncation | $[\tilde{M},\ \tilde{M} + 2\delta)$ |
| Stepped rounding through $d + 1$ decimals, halves up | $[\tilde{M} - 1.1\delta,\ \tilde{M} + 0.9\delta)$ |

: Exact means that are reported as $\tilde{M}$ under different rounding practices, for positive values. {#tbl-rounding-intervals}

The reported mean is **GRIM-consistent** if at least one attainable mean lies in the interval:

$$\mathcal{G}_{Nk} \cap I(\tilde{M}) \neq \varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\, S \in \mathbb{Z} : \frac{S}{Nk} \in I(\tilde{M}).$$

Multiplying through by $Nk$ turns this into a question about whole numbers in an interval of sums. Under the lenient rule, the reported mean is consistent if and only if

$$\left\lceil Nk\,(\tilde{M} - \delta) \right\rceil \;\le\; \left\lfloor Nk\,(\tilde{M} + \delta) \right\rfloor,$$

where $\lceil \cdot \rceil$ rounds up to the next whole number and $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$ rounds down. The left side is the smallest whole-number sum that is large enough, and the right side is the largest that is small enough. If the smallest exceeds the largest, no sum fits.

An equivalent form uses the whole number nearest to the implied sum. Writing $S^{*}$ for $Nk\,\tilde{M}$ rounded to the nearest whole number, the reported mean is consistent if and only if

$$\left| S^{*} - Nk\,\tilde{M} \right| \;\le\; Nk\,\delta .$$
:::

### Consistency rates under random means {#sec-grim-pass-rates}

Judging any GRIM result depends on one quantity. Suppose a reported value had nothing to do with any data, and was drawn at random from all the values that can be printed with *d* decimals. What is the probability that it passes GRIM?

This is the **pass rate**: the share of all printable values that the test would accept for a given design. A pass rate of 0.30 means that 30% of two-decimal values are attainable, so a wrong value picked at random has a 30% chance of slipping through. The **fail rate** is one minus the pass rate. Three properties make it useful.

-   It is a property of the design: the sample size, the number of items, the number of decimals, and the rounding rule. It does not depend on the reported value. It can be computed before looking at any results.
-   The fail rate is the test's power against a random wrong value. A value with a fail rate of 0.72 is one where a wrong number would be caught 72% of the time. A value with a fail rate of zero cannot be caught at all.
-   It defines which values are **informative**. Only values with a fail rate above zero can tell us anything, whether they pass or fail.

Brown and Heathers' Figure 1, reproduced interactively in @fig-grim-grid, shows the pass rate directly. Each column is a sample size and each row is one of the possible endings of a mean at the chosen number of decimals: 100 at two decimals. Black cells are attainable, and white cells are impossible. Small samples leave most endings impossible, and the impossible region shrinks to nothing as *N* approaches 100. The share of black cells in a column is the pass rate for that sample size. Change the number of decimals, the items averaged, and the rounding rule to see how the pattern changes. Type a mean and a sample size, or click a cell, to select it. The selected cell is outlined in blue.

::: {#fig-grim-grid}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ggMean = Inputs.number({label: "Reported mean", value: 3.12, step: 0.001, width: 90})
viewof ggN = Inputs.number({label: "Sample size (N)", value: 8, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof ggDigits = Inputs.select([1, 2, 3], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})
viewof ggItems = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof ggRounding = Inputs.select(roundingOptions, {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// which endings are attainable at every sample size shown. the plot reaches a little past the point where every ending
// is attainable, and always includes the selected sample size
ggGrid = {
  const d = ggDigits, scale = 10 ** d, k = ggItems
  if (!Number.isInteger(k) || k < 1) return null
  const cols = Math.max(10, Math.ceil(1.1 * scale / k), Number.isInteger(ggN) && ggN <= 5000 ? ggN : 0)
  // one colour per cell, in rows from the top (largest ending) down
  const fills = new Array(cols * scale), passRate = new Float64Array(cols + 1)
  for (let n = 1; n <= cols; n++) {
    const reached = grimEndings(n * k, d, ggRounding)
    let count = 0
    for (let j = 0; j < scale; j++) {
      fills[(scale - 1 - j) * cols + (n - 1)] = reached[j] ? "black" : "white"
      count += reached[j]
    }
    passRate[n] = count / scale
  }
  return {d, scale, k, cols, fills, passRate}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!ggGrid) return html`<p style="font-weight: 600;">Enter a whole number of items.</p>`
  const {d, scale, k, cols, fills, passRate} = ggGrid
  const blue = "#2780e3", red = "#c0392b", grey = "#6c757d"
  const valid = Number.isFinite(ggMean) && Number.isInteger(ggN) && ggN >= 1 && ggN <= cols
  // the selected cell: the sample size, and the ending of the mean at the chosen number of decimals
  const n = valid ? ggN : null
  const j = valid ? ((Math.round(ggMean * scale) % scale) + scale) % scale : null
  const margins = {marginLeft: 64, marginRight: 10, marginTop: 10, marginBottom: 45}
  const frame = Math.min(520, width - margins.marginLeft - margins.marginRight)
  const plotWidth = frame + margins.marginLeft + margins.marginRight
  const plotHeight = Math.round(frame * 0.7) + margins.marginTop + margins.marginBottom
  const xDomain = [0.5, cols + 0.5], yDomain = [-0.5 / scale, (scale - 0.5) / scale]
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: plotWidth, height: plotHeight, ...margins,
    x: {label: "Sample size (N)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: xDomain},
    y: {label: "Decimal part of the reported mean", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 54, domain: yDomain, ticks: 10, tickFormat: t => t.toFixed(d)},
    color: {type: "identity"},
    style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
    marks: [
      // drawn as one image, because there can be over a million cells at three decimals
      Plot.raster(fills, {width: cols, height: scale, x1: xDomain[0], x2: xDomain[1], y1: yDomain[1], y2: yDomain[0], fill: f => f, imageRendering: "pixelated"}),
      Plot.frame({stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
      valid ? Plot.rect([{}], {x1: n - 0.5, x2: n + 0.5, y1: (j - 0.5) / scale, y2: (j + 0.5) / scale, inset: -2, fill: "none", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 5}) : null,
      valid ? Plot.rect([{}], {x1: n - 0.5, x2: n + 0.5, y1: (j - 0.5) / scale, y2: (j + 0.5) / scale, inset: -2, fill: "none", stroke: blue, strokeWidth: 2.5}) : null
    ]
  })
  // clicking or dragging in the plot selects the cell under the pointer: its sample size, and its ending added to the
  // whole-number part of the current mean
  clickToSet(plot, {width: plotWidth, height: plotHeight, ...margins, xDomain, yDomain}, (x, y) => {
    const whole = Number.isFinite(ggMean) ? Math.floor(ggMean) : 0
    const ending = Math.min(scale - 1, Math.max(0, Math.round(y * scale)))
    setInput(viewof ggN, Math.min(cols, Math.max(1, Math.round(x))))
    setInput(viewof ggMean, +(whole + ending / scale).toFixed(d))
  })
  const who = `${n} participants${k > 1 ? `, each scored as the average of ${k} items,` : ""}`
  const share = valid ? passRate[n] : null
  const [verdict, colour] = !valid ? [null, null] : share === 1 ? ["GRIM-uninformative", grey] : fills[(scale - 1 - j) * cols + (n - 1)] === "black" ? ["GRIM-consistent", blue] : ["GRIM-inconsistent", red]
  const message = valid
    ? html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.2rem 0;">A mean of ${(Math.floor(ggMean) + j / scale).toFixed(d)} from ${who} is <span style="color: ${colour};">${verdict}</span>, with ${roundingPhrases[ggRounding]}.</p>
<p style="margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;">At this sample size, ${Math.round(share * 1000) / 10}% of ${d}-decimal endings are attainable.</p>`
    : html`<p style="margin: 0.8rem 0 0.5rem 0;">Enter a mean and a whole-number sample size of up to ${cols} to select a cell.</p>`
  const legendSquare = (fill, stroke) => `<svg width="14" height="14" style="vertical-align: -2px;"><rect x="1" y="1" width="12" height="12" fill="${fill}" stroke="${stroke}"/></svg>`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = `<span>${legendSquare("black", "black")} Attainable</span>
    <span>${legendSquare("white", "rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.8)")} Impossible</span>
    <span>${legendSquare("none", blue)} Selected cell</span>`
  return html`${message}${plot}${legend}`
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared by the plots of attainable endings and pass rates
roundingOptions = new Map([["Up or down", "up_or_down"], ["Half up", "up"], ["Half down", "down"], ["Half to even", "even"], ["Truncation", "trunc"], ["Up or down, or truncation", "up_or_down_trunc"]])
roundingPhrases = ({up_or_down: "halves rounded up or down", up: "halves rounded up", down: "halves rounded down", even: "halves rounded to even", trunc: "values truncated", up_or_down_trunc: "halves rounded up or down, or values truncated"})
function grimEndings(nk, d, rounding) {
  // which of the 10^d endings at d decimals some mean of nk whole numbers is reported as. only the decimal part of a
  // mean matters, so the sums S = 0 to nk - 1 cover every case. the arithmetic is in whole numbers, so that exact
  // halves stay exact: the mean S / nk is S x 10^d / nk reporting steps
  const scale = 10 ** d, reached = new Uint8Array(scale)
  const rules = {up_or_down: ["up", "down"], up_or_down_trunc: ["up", "down", "trunc"]}[rounding] ?? [rounding]
  for (let S = 0; S < nk; S++) {
    const num = S * scale, q = (num - (num % nk)) / nk, twice = 2 * (num % nk)
    for (const rule of rules) {
      // twice the remainder is above, below, or equal to nk when the mean is above, below, or exactly at a half
      const v = rule === "trunc" ? q
        : twice > nk ? q + 1 : twice < nk ? q
        : rule === "up" ? q + 1 : rule === "down" ? q : q % 2 === 0 ? q : q + 1
      reached[v % scale] = 1
    }
  }
  return reached
}
```

GRIM-consistent (black) and GRIM-inconsistent (white) endings of a mean, by sample size. Only the decimal part of a mean matters: if 2.49 is attainable for a given *N*, so are 0.49 and 8.49.
:::

Brown and Heathers give the approximation: with two decimals and *N* below 100, a random value is consistent in about *N*% of cases. More generally the pass rate is close to *N* × items / 10^*d*^, up to a maximum of 1. It is not exactly that under the lenient rounding rule, because sample sizes that produce exact halves have higher pass rates (@sec-grim-leniency).

#### The cost of leniency {#sec-grim-leniency}

Every rounding practice that the test accommodates widens the band of exact values that count as a match, so more wrong values pass. The trade-off is unavoidable: a lenient test raises fewer false alarms and misses more errors.

To see its size, we work out the pass rate under different combinations of rounding rules. For each sample size, we take every mean that whole numbers can produce, round it under each rule with the {roundwork} package (which {scrutiny} uses for its own rounding), and count how many of the 100 possible two-decimal endings are reached. For the "up" and "up or down" rules, these counts are the same as the share of endings that {scrutiny}'s `grim()` accepts. We use the same function for the pass rates in the rest of the chapter.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# the decimal parts of every mean that n * items whole-number scores can produce. only the decimal part matters for
# GRIM, so one unit's worth of sums is enough
attainable_means <- function(n, items = 1) (0:(n * items - 1)) / (n * items)

# the share of all values printable at d decimals that some attainable mean is reported as, under any of the rounding
# rules: "up" and "down" round halves up or down, and "trunc" cuts the extra decimals off. truncation cuts the stored
# binary value, so a mean of exactly 0.58, stored as 0.57999..., would be cut to 0.57. a nudge far smaller than any
# reporting step avoids this
pass_rate <- function(n, d, items = 1, rules = c("up", "down")) {
  means <- attainable_means(n, items)
  reported <- unlist(lapply(rules, \(rule) reround(if (rule == "trunc") means + 1e-9 else means, digits = d, rounding = rule)))
  endings <- round(reported * 10^d) %% 10^d  # a mean rounded up to 1.00 has the same ending as 0.00
  length(unique(endings)) / 10^d
}

# check against {scrutiny}: the share of printable endings that grim() accepts must be the same
scrutiny_pass_rate <- function(n, d, items = 1, rounding = "up_or_down") {
  mean(grim(x = 5 + (0:(10^d - 1)) / 10^d, n = n, digits_x = d, items = items, rounding = rounding))
}
pass_rate_check <- expand_grid(n = 1:110, items = c(1, 3)) |>
  mutate(up_or_down = map2_lgl(n, items, \(n, items) isTRUE(all.equal(pass_rate(n, 2, items), scrutiny_pass_rate(n, 2, items)))),
         up = map2_lgl(n, items, \(n, items) isTRUE(all.equal(pass_rate(n, 2, items, "up"), scrutiny_pass_rate(n, 2, items, "up")))))
stopifnot(all(pass_rate_check$up_or_down), all(pass_rate_check$up))
```

Here we use the pass rate to compare three versions of the test.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rounding-pass-rates
#| fig-cap: "Share of all two-decimal values that pass GRIM for a single item, by sample size, under three sets of accommodated rounding practices."
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
rounding_rules <- list(
  "Halves up only"                    = "up",
  "Halves up or down"                 = c("up", "down"),
  "Halves up or down, or truncation"  = c("up", "down", "trunc")
)

rounding_pass <- expand_grid(n = 1:110, rule = names(rounding_rules)) |>
  mutate(pass = map2_dbl(n, rule, \(n, rule) pass_rate(n, d = 2, rules = rounding_rules[[rule]])),
         rule = fct_inorder(rule))

ggplot(rounding_pass, aes(n, pass, colour = rule)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2780e3", "#e39f27", "#c0392b")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 110, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Sample size (N)", y = "Values that pass", colour = "Accommodated") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

Under the strict rule the pass rate is exactly *N*/100. Allowing halves to go either way makes no difference at most sample sizes, because exact halves only arise when the sample size is a multiple of 8. Where they do arise the effect can be large: at *N* = 40 the pass rate is 60% instead of 40%, and at *N* = 80 every value passes, so the lenient test already stops being informative there. Allowing truncation as well costs more, and at almost every sample size: the pass rate climbs about one and a half times as fast, and from about *N* = 67 nothing can fail. The exceptions are sample sizes that divide evenly into 100, such as 20, 25, and 50, where means have no further decimals to cut off.

The same idea carries over to the other tests. For percentages, the pass rate is about *N* / 10^*d*+2^. For GRIMMER, @fig-grimmer-pass-rates in @sec-grimmer shows the joint pass rate for a random mean and SD, which is far lower than for GRIM alone in small samples. {scrutiny} reports the fail rate under the strict rule as the `probability` column of `grim_map()`, and `grim_probability()` returns it directly.

Is a random number the right comparison? The pass rate assumes that a wrong value is equally likely to be any printable value. Real wrong values are not like that. A typo usually changes one digit. A value copied from the wrong row is another real mean. People who invent numbers favour some final digits and avoid others. The uniform assumption is best treated as a reference point, not a model of how errors arise, and conclusions that depend on it should be checked against other reference distributions. The `grim_sensitivity()` function in {strait} does this for digit preferences.

### When GRIM is uninformative {#sec-grim-uninformative}

The most important practical fact about GRIM is where its pass rate reaches 100%. From that point every printable value passes, the test cannot fail, and a pass tells us nothing. The test can only fail when the attainable means are further apart than the reporting steps, which requires

$$N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}$$

where *d* is the number of reported decimals. With the usual two decimals, GRIM applies to fewer than 100 participants on a single item. At or above that, every two-decimal value is attainable and every mean passes. Brown and Heathers call variables below this limit **GRIM-testable**.
Allowing halves to be rounded either way can end the test slightly earlier, at sample sizes that produce exact halves. At *N* = 80, for example, every two-decimal value passes (@sec-grim-leniency). The GRIM plot in @sec-grim-grimmer-plot reports the test as uninformative in both cases.

Use @fig-pass-rates to see where the limit falls for different numbers of decimals, items averaged, and rounding rules.

::: {#fig-pass-rates}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof prDigits = Inputs.select([1, 2, 3], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})
viewof prItems = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof prRounding = Inputs.select(roundingOptions, {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = prDigits, scale = 10 ** d, k = prItems
  if (!Number.isInteger(k) || k < 1) return html`<p style="font-weight: 600;">Enter a whole number of items.</p>`
  const blue = "#2780e3"
  const maxN = Math.max(10, Math.ceil(1.15 * scale / k))
  const rows = d3.range(1, maxN + 1).map(n => ({n, pass: grimEndings(n * k, d, prRounding).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / scale, approximation: Math.min(1, n * k / scale)}))
  // the sample size from which the test can never fail, and any smaller ones where it happens not to be able to
  let from = maxN + 1
  while (from > 1 && rows[from - 2].pass === 1) from--
  const isolated = rows.filter(r => r.n < from && r.pass === 1).map(r => r.n)
  const margins = {marginLeft: 64, marginRight: 28, marginTop: 20, marginBottom: 45}
  const frame = Math.min(520, width - margins.marginLeft - margins.marginRight)
  const plotWidth = frame + margins.marginLeft + margins.marginRight
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: plotWidth, height: Math.round(frame * 0.6) + margins.marginTop + margins.marginBottom, ...margins,
    x: {label: "Sample size (N)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: [0, maxN]},
    y: {label: "Values that pass", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 54, domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "n", y: "approximation", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "n", y: "pass", stroke: blue, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      from <= maxN ? Plot.ruleX([from], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6}) : null,
      from <= maxN ? Plot.text([{}], {x: from, y: 1, text: () => `N = ${from}`, dy: -8, textAnchor: from > maxN * 0.8 ? "end" : "start", dx: from > maxN * 0.8 ? -4 : 4, fontWeight: 600}) : null,
      Plot.dot(isolated.map(n => ({n})), {x: "n", y: () => 1, r: 4, fill: blue})
    ]
  })
  const what = `With ${d} ${d === 1 ? "decimal" : "decimals"}, ${k} ${k === 1 ? "item" : "items"} averaged, and ${roundingPhrases[prRounding]}`
  const also = isolated.length ? `, and also at N = ${isolated.length > 6 ? isolated.slice(0, 6).join(", ") + ", …" : isolated.join(", ")}` : ""
  const message = from <= 1 ? `${what}, GRIM cannot fail at any sample size.` : `${what}, GRIM cannot fail from N = ${from} onwards${also}.`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = `<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="${blue}" stroke-width="2"/></svg> Pass rate</span>
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.5" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/></svg> Approximation, <i>N</i> × items / 10<sup><i>d</i></sup></span>`
  return html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.5rem 0;">${message}</p>${plot}${legend}`
}
```

GRIM pass rates by sample size, for the chosen number of decimals, items averaged, and rounding rule. The dashed line is the approximation *N* × items / 10^*d*^. The vertical line marks the sample size from which GRIM can no longer fail.
:::

Changing the number of decimals or the items averaged does not change the shape of the line, because only the product *N* × items matters. It only changes where the line reaches 100%: at *N* = 10 for a single item reported to one decimal, and at *N* = 1,000 for a single item reported to three. A five-item mean score at two decimals is exhausted by *N* = 20, and a ten-item mean score at one decimal cannot be tested at any sample size.

Two consequences follow.

**Decimals matter as much as sample size.** Each extra reported decimal multiplies the reach of the test by ten. A mean reported to three decimals is testable up to *N* = 999, and one reported to a single decimal only up to *N* = 9. Supplementary tables, which often report more decimals than the main text, are therefore worth checking.

**Record every value exactly as printed.** "3.50" has two decimals and "3.5" has one, and GRIM gives different answers for them. Spreadsheets and statistical software drop trailing zeros silently, so the number of decimals has to be recorded when the value is read from the article. It cannot be recovered afterwards from a stored number.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths of when GRIM cannot be used

In units of the sum, the interval $Nk \times I(\tilde{M})$ has width

$$2\,\delta\,Nk = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}}.$$

An interval of width 1 or more that includes at least one of its ends always contains a whole number. So whenever $Nk \ge 10^{d}$, every reported value is consistent and the test cannot fail. This is the condition $N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}$ given above.

When $Nk < 10^{d}$, neighbouring attainable means are more than one reporting step apart, so each rounds to a different reported value. The $Nk$ attainable means in any unit interval, such as from 3.00 up to 4.00, therefore account for exactly $Nk$ of the $10^{d}$ values that can be printed there. Under a strict rounding rule, the share of printable values that are consistent is

$$p = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}},$$

and the share that are inconsistent is $q = 1 - p$. These are the pass rate and fail rate described in @sec-grim-pass-rates. Under the lenient rule, an attainable mean that falls exactly halfway between two printable values makes both of them consistent, so $p$ is larger by one printable value for each such tie.

A percentage reported to $d$ decimals is a proportion reported to $d + 2$ decimals, with $k = 1$. Everything above applies with $d + 2$ in place of $d$.
:::

### Interpreting a consistent result {#sec-grim-interpreting}

A failure and a pass are not mirror images. A failure shows that something among the reported mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding is not as stated (@sec-grim-errors). A pass only shows that the mean was not caught, and what that is worth depends on how likely a wrong value would have been to be caught.

The pass rate answers this, because it describes the counterfactual of a value that has nothing to do with the data. Suppose a mean from 12 participants passes GRIM. A value picked at random would have passed only about 12% of the time, so the pass rules out most ways of being wrong. Now suppose a mean from 90 participants passes. A random value would have passed about 90% of the time, so the pass is almost exactly what we would expect whether the mean was correct or not. From 100 participants on, a pass carries no information at all.

A consistent result is therefore best reported as "not shown to be impossible", together with its pass rate, and never as evidence that a value is correct. The same holds for a set of values: ten random values would all pass at *N* = 90 about a third of the time, but three would all pass at *N* = 12 less than once in 500 tries.

## GRIMMER: Testing consistency among N/M/SD/integer data {#sec-grimmer}

When an article reports the SD alongside the mean, a second test becomes possible. GRIMMER asks whether any set of *N* whole numbers could produce the reported mean and the reported SD together. The test was introduced by @anaya2016, who found the patterns that attainable variances follow by simulation. @allard2018 then showed that the same test can be derived with simple algebra. The implementation in {scrutiny} follows the analytic version.

@brown2017 open their article with a fictional example. Participants were randomly assigned to drink water that either did (*N* = 28) or did not (*N* = 27) contain Kool-Aid powder, and then answered the question "To what extent do you believe that pigs can fly?" on a scale from 1 to 7. Those who drank the Kool-Aid reported *M* = 5.19, *SD* = 1.34. That mean already fails GRIM: 5.19 × 28 = 145.32, and the attainable means on either side are 145/28 = 5.179 and 146/28 = 5.214. If the mean had been reported as the attainable 5.21, would the SD be possible? GRIMMER answers questions like this.

The SD is calculated from the sum of the squared scores. When the scores are whole numbers, that sum of squares must itself be a whole number. It must also be odd when the sum of the scores is odd, and even when the sum is even, because squaring a whole number never changes whether it is odd or even. GRIMMER applies these two facts.

1.  Run GRIM. If the mean is impossible, stop. Otherwise GRIM has identified the sum of the scores.
2.  The reported SD stands for a small range of exact values, because it was rounded. Turn that range into a range for the sum of squares.
3.  Check whether the range contains a whole number, and whether that whole number is odd or even as required.

For example, with a mean of 3.50 from 10 participants, a reported SD of 1.20 or 1.22 is impossible, but 1.18 is possible. The box below works through why.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths: GRIMMER

Rearranging the usual formula for the sample SD gives the sum of the squared scores:

$$\sum x^2 = (N - 1) \times SD^2 + \frac{\left(\sum x\right)^2}{N}$$

The left-hand side is a sum of squared whole numbers, so it must be a whole number, with the same parity (odd or even) as $\sum x$. Step 2 above puts the lowest and highest exact SD that round to the reported value into the right-hand side, to give the range that $\sum x^2$ must lie in.

Take a mean of 3.50 from 10 participants, so that the sum is 35, an odd number. For a reported SD of 1.20, the exact SD lies between 1.195 and 1.205, and the sum of squares between 9 × 1.195² + 122.5 = 135.35 and 9 × 1.205² + 122.5 = 135.57. No whole number lies in that range, so the SD is impossible. For a reported SD of 1.22, the range is 135.79 to 136.01. It contains 136, but 136 is even and the sum is odd, so this SD is impossible too. A reported SD of 1.18 gives a range of 134.93 to 135.14, which contains 135, an odd number. That SD is possible.

For a mean score across $k$ items, each participant's total across the items is a whole number, so the same argument applies to the sum of the squared totals, $k^2 \left[(N - 1) \times SD^2 + N \times M^2\right]$.
:::

```{r}
grimmer(x = 3.50, sd = c(1.20, 1.22, 1.18), n = 10, digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2)
```

Returning to the Kool-Aid example: if the mean had been reported as the attainable 5.21, would the *SD* of 1.34 be possible?

```{r}
grimmer(x = 5.21, sd = 1.34, n = 28, digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2)
```

It would.

### Visualising GRIM and GRIMMER together {#sec-grim-grimmer-plot}

When the *SD* is reported as well, the same idea extends to a second dimension. The plot below adds the *SD* on the vertical axis. It shows every pair of a mean and an *SD*, as they would be printed to the chosen number of decimals, around the mean and the *SD* that you enter. The zoom setting chooses how far the plot reaches on either side of them: 1 at low zoom, 0.5 at medium, and 0.25 at high. The rounding setting applies to the mean and the *SD* alike. Each pair is a small square. It is black if some set of *N* whole numbers could produce that mean and *SD*, and white if no set could. A white column is a mean that fails GRIM, and no *SD* can rescue it. White squares inside an otherwise black column are *SD*s that fail GRIMMER, the test for the *SD* described in @sec-grimmer. Typing a mean or an *SD* centres the plot on it. Clicking or dragging in the plot chooses a pair without moving the plot. The chosen pair is circled in blue.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof grimMean = Inputs.number({label: "Reported mean", value: 5.19, step: 0.01, width: 90})
viewof grimSd = Inputs.number({label: "Reported SD", value: 1.34, step: 0.01, min: 0, width: 90})
viewof grimN = Inputs.range([2, 100], {label: "Sample size (N)", step: 1, value: 28})
viewof grimDigits = Inputs.select([1, 2], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})
viewof grimItems = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof grimRounding = Inputs.select(new Map([["Up or down", "up_or_down"], ["Half up", "up"]]), {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})
viewof grimZoom = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Low", 1], ["Medium", 0.5], ["High", 0.25]]), {label: "Zoom", value: 0.5})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// the centre of the plot. it moves to the mean and SD when either is typed in, and stays put when they are chosen by
// clicking or dragging in the plot, or when anything else changes
grimView = ({mean: 5.19, sd: 1.34, recentre: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  // typing fires an input event on the text box itself, whereas clicking in the plot sets the value on the whole input
  for (const view of [viewof grimMean, viewof grimSd]) {
    view.querySelector("input").addEventListener("input", () => { grimView.recentre = true })
  }
  return html``
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
grimCalc = {
  const d = grimDigits, scale = 10 ** d
  const n = grimN, k = grimItems, nk = n * k
  if (!Number.isFinite(grimMean) || !Number.isFinite(grimSd) || grimSd < 0 || !Number.isInteger(k) || k < 1) return {valid: false}
  // values are handled as whole numbers of reporting steps, so that 5.19 at two decimals is 519
  const ix = Math.round(grimMean * scale), iy = Math.round(grimSd * scale)
  // a value exactly halfway between two reported values may be rounded either way ("up or down"), or only up
  // ("half up"), in which case the top of its interval is excluded. this applies to the mean and the SD alike
  const halfUp = grimRounding === "up"
  // GRIM: the whole-number sums S whose mean, S / (N x items), is reported as i / scale
  const sumsFor = i => {
    const top = nk * (i + 0.5) / scale
    return d3.range(Math.ceil(nk * (i - 0.5) / scale - 1e-9), (halfUp ? Math.ceil(top - 1e-9) - 1 : Math.floor(top + 1e-9)) + 1)
  }
  // GRIMMER, given a sum S: the sum of the squared per-participant totals, Q = items^2 (N - 1) SD^2 + S^2 / N, must
  // be a whole number that is odd when S is odd and even when S is even. the SD is the sample SD
  const sdFits = (S, j) => {
    const sdLo = Math.max(j - 0.5, 0) / scale, sdHi = (j + 0.5) / scale
    const lower = k * k * (n - 1) * sdLo ** 2 + S * S / n
    const upper = k * k * (n - 1) * sdHi ** 2 + S * S / n
    const eps = 1e-9 * Math.max(1, upper)
    let q = Math.ceil(lower - eps)
    if (Math.abs(q - S) % 2 === 1) q += 1
    return halfUp ? q < upper - eps : q <= upper + eps
  }
  const v = grimView
  if (v.recentre) Object.assign(v, {mean: grimMean, sd: grimSd, recentre: false})
  // the plot reaches the zoom distance (1, 0.5, or 0.25) below and above the centre on both axes, and always at
  // least one reporting step
  const half = Math.max(1, Math.round(grimZoom * scale)), size = 2 * half + 1
  const i0 = Math.round(v.mean * scale) - half, j0 = Math.round(v.sd * scale) - half
  const columnSums = d3.range(size).map(c => sumsFor(i0 + c))
  // one colour per square, in rows from the top (largest SD) down. SDs below zero are left empty
  const fills = new Array(size * size)
  for (let r = 0; r < size; r++) {
    const j = j0 + size - 1 - r
    for (let c = 0; c < size; c++) {
      fills[r * size + c] = j < 0 ? null : columnSums[c].some(S => sdFits(S, j)) ? "black" : "white"
    }
  }
  const selectedSums = sumsFor(ix)
  const result = selectedSums.length === 0 ? "grim" : selectedSums.some(S => sdFits(S, iy)) ? "ok" : "grimmer"
  return {valid: true, d, scale, nk, ix, iy, i0, j0, size, fills, result}
}
```

```{ojs}
  const legendSquare = (fill, stroke) => `<svg width="14" height="14" style="vertical-align: -2px;"><rect x="1" y="1" width="12" height="12" fill="${fill}" stroke="${stroke}"/></svg>`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`

  return html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.2rem 0;">${message}</p>
<p style="margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;">Attainable means are ${(1 / nk).toFixed(4)} apart${nk >= 10 ** d ? `, which is no wider than the ${d}-decimal reporting steps, so no mean can fail GRIM` : ""}.</p>
${plot}${legend}`
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// helpers for the plot above
function clickToSet(plot, {width, height, marginLeft, marginRight, marginTop, marginBottom, xDomain, yDomain}, onPick) {
  // calls onPick(x, y) with the data coordinates of a click inside the plot's frame, and again as the pointer is
  // dragged. each call redraws the plot, which replaces this element, so the drag is followed on the window rather
  // than on the plot, using the position and size the plot had when the drag began
  plot.style.cursor = "crosshair"
  plot.style.touchAction = "none"
  plot.addEventListener("pointerdown", down => {
    const box = plot.getBoundingClientRect()
    const toData = event => {
      const px = (event.clientX - box.left) * width / box.width, py = (event.clientY - box.top) * height / box.height
      const fx = (px - marginLeft) / (width - marginLeft - marginRight), fy = 1 - (py - marginTop) / (height - marginTop - marginBottom)
      return {fx, fy, x: xDomain[0] + fx * (xDomain[1] - xDomain[0]), y: yDomain[0] + fy * (yDomain[1] - yDomain[0])}
    }
    const start = toData(down)
    if (start.fx < 0 || start.fx > 1 || start.fy < 0 || start.fy > 1) return
    down.preventDefault()
    onPick(start.x, start.y)
    // while dragging, the selection follows the pointer, held inside the frame, with at most one update per frame
    let pending = null
    const move = event => {
      if (pending === null) requestAnimationFrame(() => {
        const {fx, fy} = toData(pending)
        const cx = Math.min(0.999, Math.max(0.001, fx)), cy = Math.min(0.999, Math.max(0.001, fy))
        onPick(xDomain[0] + cx * (xDomain[1] - xDomain[0]), yDomain[0] + cy * (yDomain[1] - yDomain[0]))
        pending = null
      })
      pending = event
    }
    const up = () => {
      window.removeEventListener("pointermove", move)
      window.removeEventListener("pointerup", up)
      window.removeEventListener("pointercancel", up)
      document.body.style.cursor = ""
    }
    document.body.style.cursor = "crosshair"
    window.addEventListener("pointermove", move)
    window.addEventListener("pointerup", up)
    window.addEventListener("pointercancel", up)
  })
}
function setInput(view, value) {
  // set an input's value and tell everything that depends on it
  view.value = value
  view.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
}
```

The default values are the Kool-Aid example above: a mean of 5.19 and an *SD* of 1.34 from 28 participants. Each white square in the GRIM plot in @sec-grim-grimmer-plot becomes a white column here, because a mean that fails GRIM fails whatever the *SD*. Raise *N* towards 100 and the white columns disappear as before, but white squares among the black columns last longer, especially where the *SD* is small, because GRIMMER can still fail where GRIM no longer can.

### How much does GRIMMER add?

GRIMMER catches impossible SDs when the mean is fine, which GRIM cannot do. How often it does so depends on something GRIM is indifferent to: the size of the SD. The range in step 2 gets wider as the SD gets larger, and a wider range is more likely to contain a suitable whole number. @anaya2016 noted that the test is most powerful when the SD is small.

@fig-grimmer-pass-rates measures this. With "GRIMMER SD test only" selected, it shows GRIMMER's own contribution: the mean is correct, so the sum is known, and we ask what share of SD values near a given magnitude would pass. With "GRIMMER mean + SD tests" selected, it shows the two tests together: the share of pairs of a mean and an SD that pass both. The other settings work as in @fig-pass-rates.

::: {#fig-grimmer-pass-rates}

```{ojs}

viewof gmItems = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof gmRounding = Inputs.select(roundingOptions, {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = gmDigits, scale = 10 ** d, k = gmItems
  if (!Number.isInteger(k) || k < 1) return html`<p style="font-weight: 600;">Enter a whole number of items.</p>`
  const bands = [{mid: 0.5, colour: "#2780e3"}, {mid: 1, colour: "#27b3e3"}, {mid: 2, colour: "#e39f27"}, {mid: 3, colour: "#c0392b"}]
  // up to `count` whole numbers spread evenly from lo to hi
  const evenly = (lo, hi, count) => hi - lo + 1 <= count ? d3.range(lo, hi + 1) : d3.range(count).map(t => lo + Math.round(t * (hi - lo) / (count - 1)))
  // sample sizes up to four times the point at which GRIM stops being able to fail
  const maxN = Math.max(20, Math.ceil(4 * scale / k))
  const ns = [...new Set(evenly(2, maxN, 60))]
  // the means tested together with the SD: every ending at one or two decimals, and 100 spread over the 1,000 at three
  const endings = scale <= 100 ? d3.range(scale) : d3.range(100).map(t => (t * 37) % scale)
  const rows = []
  for (const n of ns) {
    const nk = n * k
    // for the SD test only, the mean is taken to be correct, so the sum is known: 100 sums spread over a 1 to 7 scale
    const sumSets = gmTest === "sd" ? evenly(nk, 7 * nk, 100).map(S => [S]) : endings.map(e => grimmerSums(3 * scale + e, nk, scale, gmRounding))
    for (const {mid} of bands) {
      // SDs within 0.25 of the stated value, at most 50 of them
      const js = evenly(Math.round((mid - 0.25) * scale), Math.round((mid + 0.25) * scale) - 1, 50)
      let pass = 0
      for (const sums of sumSets) for (const j of js) pass += sums.some(S => grimmerSdFits(S, j, n, k, scale, gmRounding))
      rows.push({n, band: `SD near ${mid}`, pass: pass / (sumSets.length * js.length)})
    }
    rows.push({n, band: "GRIM alone", pass: grimEndings(nk, d, gmRounding).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / scale})
  }
  // the sample size from which each line stays at 100%
  const settles = band => { const r = rows.filter(x => x.band === band); let t = r.length; while (t > 0 && r[t - 1].pass === 1) t--; return t === r.length ? null : r[t].n }
  const margins = {marginLeft: 64, marginRight: 28, marginTop: 20, marginBottom: 45}
  const frame = Math.min(520, width - margins.marginLeft - margins.marginRight)
  const plotWidth = frame + margins.marginLeft + margins.marginRight
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: plotWidth, height: Math.round(frame * 0.6) + margins.marginTop + margins.marginBottom, ...margins,
    x: {label: "Sample size (N)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: [0, maxN]},
    y: {label: "Values that pass", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 54, domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows.filter(r => r.band === "GRIM alone"), {x: "n", y: "pass", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      ...bands.map(({mid, colour}) => Plot.lineY(rows.filter(r => r.band === `SD near ${mid}`), {x: "n", y: "pass", stroke: colour, strokeWidth: 1.5}))
    ]
  })
  const where = band => { const n = settles(band); return n === null ? `not by N = ${maxN}` : n <= 2 ? "at any sample size" : `from about N = ${n}` }
  // for GRIM, every sample size is checked, as in the plot of GRIM pass rates, so that the two plots agree
  let grimFrom = maxN + 1
  while (grimFrom > 1 && grimEndings((grimFrom - 1) * k, d, gmRounding).every(x => x === 1)) grimFrom--
  const what = `With ${d} ${d === 1 ? "decimal" : "decimals"}, ${k} ${k === 1 ? "item" : "items"} averaged, and ${roundingPhrases[gmRounding]}`
  const message = `${what}, GRIM cannot fail ${grimFrom <= 1 ? "at any sample size" : grimFrom > maxN ? `by N = ${maxN}` : `from N = ${grimFrom} onwards`}. ${gmTest === "sd" ? "The SD test on its own" : "The mean and SD tests together"} stop${gmTest === "sd" ? "s" : ""} being able to fail ${where("SD near 0.5")} for SDs near 0.5, and ${where("SD near 1")} for SDs near 1.`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = bands.map(({mid, colour}) => `<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="${colour}" stroke-width="2"/></svg> SD near ${mid}</span>`).join("") +
    `<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.5" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/></svg> GRIM alone</span>`
  return html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.5rem 0;">${message}</p>${plot}${legend}`
}
```
