```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// GRIMMER for every rounding option, shared by the plot of GRIMMER pass rates
roundingRules = rounding => ({up_or_down: ["up", "down"], up_or_down_trunc: ["up", "down", "trunc"]}[rounding] ?? [rounding])
function reportedSteps(num, den, rule) {
  // a non-negative exact value num / den, in reporting steps, as it would be reported under one rule. whole-number
  // arithmetic, so that exact halves stay exact
  const q = (num - (num % den)) / den, twice = 2 * (num % den)
  return rule === "trunc" ? q
    : twice > den ? q + 1 : twice < den ? q
    : rule === "up" ? q + 1 : rule === "down" ? q : q % 2 === 0 ? q : q + 1
}
function grimmerSums(i, nk, scale, rounding) {
  // the whole-number sums whose mean, S / nk, is reported as i steps under any rule of the rounding option
  const rules = roundingRules(rounding), sums = []
  for (let S = Math.max(0, Math.floor((i - 1) * nk / scale)); S <= Math.ceil((i + 1) * nk / scale); S++) {
    if (rules.some(rule => reportedSteps(S * scale, nk, rule) === i)) sums.push(S)
  }
  return sums
}
function grimmerSdFits(S, j, n, k, scale, rounding) {
  // can a whole-number sum of squared participant totals, Q, with the parity of S, give a sample SD reported as j steps?
  // each rule gives the interval of exact SDs (in steps) that are reported as j, and whether each end is included
  return roundingRules(rounding).some(rule => {
    let [lo, hi, loIn, hiIn] = rule === "trunc" ? [j, j + 1, true, false]
      : rule === "up" ? [j - 0.5, j + 0.5, true, false]
      : rule === "down" ? [j - 0.5, j + 0.5, false, true]
      : j % 2 === 0 ? [j - 0.5, j + 0.5, true, true] : [j - 0.5, j + 0.5, false, false]
    if (lo < 0) [lo, loIn] = [0, true]
    const base = S * S / n, lower = k * k * (n - 1) * (lo / scale) ** 2 + base, upper = k * k * (n - 1) * (hi / scale) ** 2 + base
    const eps = 1e-9 * Math.max(1, upper)
    let q = loIn ? Math.ceil(lower - eps) : Math.floor(lower + eps) + 1
    if (Math.abs(q - S) % 2 === 1) q += 1
    return hiIn ? q <= upper + eps : q < upper - eps
  })
}
```

Pass rates for GRIMMER by sample size, for the chosen test, number of decimals, items averaged, and rounding rule. Each coloured line is the share of *SD*s within 0.25 of the stated value that pass. With the SD test only, the mean is taken to be correct, so the sum of the scores is known. With both tests, each pair of a mean and an *SD* must pass both. The dashed line is GRIM alone.
:::

The SD test on its own has a simple reading. For two-decimal reporting, the share of SD values that pass is close to *N* × SD / 100. With an SD near 1, the SD check is about as demanding as GRIM is for the mean. With an SD near 0.5, it is twice as demanding and still rejects some values at *N* = 300, well past the point where GRIM gives up. With an SD near 2 or 3, it passes everything from about *N* = 55 or *N* = 35.

The two tests together show what this means for the pair. For small samples the two checks multiply: at *N* = 30 and an SD near 1, about 30% of means pass GRIM but under 10% of mean and SD pairs pass both. GRIMMER is therefore a much sharper test than GRIM for small samples, and the only one of the two that can still fail above *N* = 100, provided the SD is small. Small SDs on whole-number data are common where responses pile up at one end of a scale, which is also where the bounds methods of the next chapter are most useful.

## What large-scale applications have found {#sec-grim-evidence}

::: big-number
[36 of 71]{.number}

[GRIM-testable psychology articles contained at least one mean that was inconsistent with its reported sample size [@brown2017].]{.description}
:::

The only systematic application of GRIM to a sample of the literature that we know of is in the article that introduced it. @brown2017 searched the 2011--2015 issues of *Psychological Science*, the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, and the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* for articles containing the word "Likert", and examined 260 of them. Of these, 189 (73%) had no GRIM-testable data, mostly because their samples were too large. In the remaining 71:

-   35 (49%) reported all testable means consistently.
-   15 (21%) had one or two inconsistencies that looked like typographical errors.
-   5 (7%) had a small number of inconsistencies that might affect the main results.
-   16 (23%) had a larger number of inconsistencies, often at several points in the article. In some of these, more than half of the testable values were inconsistent.

The authors requested the data for the 21 articles in the last two categories. They obtained data from eight authors, and a ninth provided enough information to check the means. Five authors refused, four promised data that did not arrive, and the rest could not be reached or did not reply. In all nine cases that could be checked, GRIM had identified at least one real problem, and three articles needed formal corrections.

The causes they found in these nine articles are instructive, because none of them is fraud and most are mundane: sample sizes that differed from those reported (in five of the nine cases), a spreadsheet formula that included the wrong cells, values copied incorrectly, the stepped rounding of SDs described in @nte-grim-rounding, and, in one case, an analysis error serious enough for the authors to issue a correction once they noticed it while preparing the data. In one case, Brown and Heathers had themselves made an error by overlooking that a measure was a multi-item composite.

The nine were the articles whose authors cooperated. The other twelve, whose authors refused the request for data, did not send it, or did not reply, were left unresolved in the published article. A later preprint by one of its authors reports what Brown and Heathers had concluded about them [@heathers2024]. All twelve contained multiple inconsistencies, and three contained what the authors considered definite hallmarks of systematic data manipulation. These figures were removed from the 2017 article because they were judged "sufficiently speculative and controversial at the time of publication". Taken together, they put the share of the 71 GRIM-testable articles with hallmarks of data manipulation at between 3 of 71 (4.2%) and 12 of 71 (16.9%). The range is wide for two reasons. A refusal to share data is not in itself evidence of manipulation, and the three clearest cases rest on the authors' judgement of the reported values, without the data that would settle them.

Granularity tests also became known through case studies. GRIM and GRIMMER were among the tools used in the reanalysis of four articles from the Cornell Food and Brand Lab [@vanderzee2017].

## Assumptions and sources of false positives and false negatives {#sec-grim-errors}

The previous sections introduced the assumptions of granularity tests one at a time. @tbl-grim-assumptions collects them. A **false positive** is a correctly reported value that the test flags as impossible. A **false negative** is an incorrect value that the test passes.

| Assumption | If it is wrong | Guard against it by |
|---------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| The *N* behind this statistic is the one we used | False positives. Cell sizes assumed equal when they are not, *N* before exclusions used in place of *N* analysed, item-level missing data | Looking for cell sizes in tables, degrees of freedom, and flow diagrams. Searching for an *N* that makes all values consistent |
| The number of items averaged into each participant's score is right | False positives if a mean score is tested as a single item. False negatives if a sum score is tested as a mean score, or if the number of items in the scale is used for a sum score | Reading the measures section for how the scale was scored. Items averaged is 1 for single items, whole-number variables, and sum scores |
| The data are whole numbers | False positives | Checking the response format |
| The mean is a simple average of observed scores, not a model estimate | False positives. Estimated marginal means, least-squares means, covariate-adjusted means, and conditional means or predicted values from a regression or mixed model are not averages of whole numbers, even when the raw scores are | Reading table notes and the analysis section for words such as adjusted, estimated, marginal, model-based, or predicted. Testing only raw descriptive means |
| No missing values were imputed | False positives. Mean imputation, regression imputation, and multiple imputation produce values that are not whole numbers, and a mean pooled over several imputed datasets is an average of means. Methods that copy observed values, such as last observation carried forward, keep whole numbers but change which *N* applies | Reading the missing-data section. Comparing the *N* analysed with the number who completed the measure. Testing complete-case statistics where they are reported |
| The rounding practice is one we allowed for | False positives | Using the lenient rule, and considering truncation and stepped rounding before reporting a failure |
| The value was extracted correctly | False positives. Dropped trailing zeros, values read from the wrong column, PDF conversion faults, the assessor's own typos | Re-reading every flagged value in the original article |
| The SD uses the sample formula, dividing by *N* − 1 (GRIMMER) | False positives. An SD calculated with the population formula, dividing by *N* (the default in NumPy, and Excel's `STDEV.P`), is smaller by a factor of √((*N* − 1)/*N*), which is enough to change the second decimal | Re-testing with the reported SDs multiplied by √(*N*/(*N* − 1)) |

: Assumptions of granularity tests and what happens when they fail. {#tbl-grim-assumptions}

False negatives have a different set of causes, most of which cannot be fixed.

-   **The test cannot fail.** When *N* × items is 100 or more at two decimals, GRIM passes everything.
-   **Chance.** A wrong value can land on an attainable one. For a wrong value picked at random, the probability is the pass rate (@sec-grim-pass-rates).
-   **Leniency.** Every accommodated rounding practice lets more wrong values through.

The asymmetry between the two outcomes is the main thing to take from this section. A failure is strong evidence that something is misreported, provided the checks in @tbl-grim-assumptions have been made, and no evidence about what or why. A pass is weak evidence of anything. Brown and Heathers make the same point: the number of GRIM failures in an article is a conservative estimate of the number of errors.

## Other granularity methods: GRIM-U {#sec-grim-u}

Granularity is not restricted to means and SDs of integer data. Any statistic that is calculated from a finite number of discrete outcomes can take only a finite set of values, so many other granularity tests could in principle be developed. Means and SDs were simply the first applications.

GRIM-U [@heathers2025] applied the principle to the Mann-Whitney U test. It relies on the granularity not of the data, which could be continuous, but of the ranks that the test calculates, and so of its U statistic and *p*-value. The test ranks all the observations from two groups and counts, for every pair made of one observation from each group, which group's member ranks higher. The U statistic is that count. 

Rank tests are a good target because they are used where samples are small and data are not normal: animal studies, pilot trials, and small clinical samples. These are the conditions under which granularity is coarse and the test can fail.

Hussey subsequently formalised an analytic form of GRIM-U, which does not need to enumerate every possible ranking, and implemented it in the {analyticgrimu} R package [@hussey2026analyticgrimu]. For the moment, this chapter does not attempt to explain analytic GRIM-U in any detail, or examine the sample sizes at which its results are informative, or consider the complexities of (assumed) maximum number of ties, etc. GRIM-U is still in early development; this content might be added later. Right now, the point is merely to highlight that other granularity methods do or could exist, and that this is an area of active research in methods development.

### Additional assumptions

GRIM-U needs more assumptions than GRIM, because a Mann-Whitney *p*-value can be calculated in several ways. Software may use the exact distribution or a normal approximation, with or without a continuity correction, and with or without a correction for ties. Exact *p*-values are also defined in more than one way. Sidedness matters too. {analyticgrimu} treats these as GRIM treats rounding: a reported result passes if *any* modelled convention reproduces it.

Ties are the largest source of leniency. Ties shrink the variance of U, so the same U can give a range of *p*-values depending on how heavily tied the data were. The package computes that range exactly and accepts anything inside it, so a correctly reported result from tied data is never flagged. The price is that the default test is weak. Checking a *p*-value on its own will almost never flag anything, and detection is one-sided: a *p*-value that is too large for its U can be caught, but one that is too small can always be explained by supposing more ties.

Two features recover some of the lost ground. If the measure is known to be continuous, or to have a known number of scale points, this can be stated, and the accepted range narrows. The share of three-decimal *p*-values that are attainable for two groups of six falls from 94% when any ties are allowed to 7% when there are none.

```{r}
grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3)
grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3, ties = "none")
```

These options are safe in one direction only. If the data were more tied than was assumed, correct results will be flagged, so it is better to err towards allowing ties. The function also reports the minimum amount of tying that a consistent explanation would require. A result that is only possible if half the sample shares one value is unremarkable for a single five-point item and not credible for a reaction time.

One coverage gap remains. Some software computes an exact permutation *p*-value conditional on the observed pattern of ties, which cannot be reconstructed from the group sizes. A failure against a result produced that way may reflect the gap and not an error.

@heathers2025 demonstrate GRIM-U on four published medical studies. No large-scale applications of GRIM-U have been conducted to date.

## Test yourself

Answer all the questions, then click the button below the quiz to see why each answer is right. Unless a question says otherwise, values are reported to two decimals, each participant answers a single question with a whole number, and halves may be rounded up or down.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**What GRIM and GRIMMER are for**

1.  Forensic methods are often divided into tests of possibility and tests of plausibility. Which kind of test is GRIM? `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = "A possibility test", "A plausibility test", "Both", "Neither"))`
2.  GRIM checks whether a reported mean could have been produced by *N* whole-number scores. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
3.  GRIMMER can show that a reported *SD* is impossible even when the reported mean passes GRIM. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
4.  A GRIM failure shows that the authors fabricated their data. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`

**A mean outside the scale.** A study collects ratings from 10 participants on a 1--7 scale, and reports their mean as 12.10.

5.  GRIM flags this mean as inconsistent. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
6.  This mean could have come from the data described. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`

**Assumptions**

7.  A 12-item questionnaire is scored by adding up each participant's answers. What number of items averaged should GRIM use? `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = "1", "12", "144", "It depends on the sample size"))`
8.  The same questionnaire is instead scored as the mean of the 12 items, in a sample of 15. GRIM can detect an error in the reported mean of these scores. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
9.  Estimated marginal means from an ANCOVA can be tested with GRIM, as long as the raw scores were whole numbers. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
10. A mean of 3.12 from 8 participants is GRIM-consistent whichever way halves were rounded. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`

**Sample size and informativeness**

11. A mean age in years from 120 participants is reported to two decimals. GRIM can detect an error in this mean. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
12. A mean from 90 participants passes GRIM. Roughly what share of two-decimal values picked at random would also pass? `r webexercises::mcq(c("10%", "50%", answer = "90%", "100%"))`
13. Because the mean from 90 participants passed GRIM, there is good evidence that it was reported correctly. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
14. A mean from 12 participants that passes GRIM tells us more than a mean from 90 participants that passes GRIM. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
15. With 150 participants, GRIMMER can still find an impossible *SD* even though GRIM can no longer fail. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
:::

`r webexercises::hide("Why is each answer right?")`

1.  **A possibility test.** GRIM asks whether a reported mean can exist at all, given the sample size and whole-number data. It does not ask whether the result is surprising or unlikely, which is what plausibility tests do. See the chapter on organising principles.
2.  **True.** That is the whole test: some whole-number sum, divided by *N* × items and rounded, must give the reported mean (@sec-grim).
3.  **True.** GRIMMER adds a second check, on the sum of the squared scores, which must be a whole number with the same parity (odd or even) as the sum of the scores. An *SD* can fail this check even when the mean is fine (@sec-grimmer).
4.  **False.** A failure shows that the mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding cannot all be as stated. It does not say which one is wrong, or why. In the largest application of GRIM, the causes found were mundane: wrong sample sizes, spreadsheet errors, values copied incorrectly, and stepped rounding (@sec-grim-evidence).
5.  **False.** 12.10 × 10 = 121, a whole number, so the mean is GRIM-consistent. GRIM only looks at the grid of attainable means. It knows nothing about the scale's minimum and maximum.
6.  **False.** On a 1--7 scale, no mean can be above 7. The value is impossible, but for a reason GRIM cannot see. Checks that use the scale's limits are the subject of the next chapter, on bounds methods.
7.  **1.** Each participant's sum is a whole number, so a sum score behaves like a single item, however many items were added up. The number of items only enters the test when each participant's answers are averaged first (@sec-grim-integer-data).
8.  **False.** With each participant's score averaged over 12 items, the mean moves in steps of 1/(15 × 12) = 1/180. That is finer than the two-decimal reporting steps, so every two-decimal mean is attainable and the test cannot fail.
9.  **False.** Model-based estimates such as estimated marginal means, covariate-adjusted means, and predicted values are not simple averages of the observed scores. Testing them with GRIM produces false positives (@tbl-grim-assumptions).
10. **False.** The only candidate sum is 25, and 25/8 = 3.125 exactly. Rounded half up, that is 3.13, so 3.12 fails. It passes only if halves can be rounded down, which is why the lenient rule counts it as consistent (@nte-grim-rounding).
11. **False.** With a single item and 100 or more participants, attainable means are no further apart than the reporting steps of 0.01, so every two-decimal mean passes. The test is uninformative here (@sec-grim-uninformative).
12. **90%.** With two decimals and fewer than 100 participants on a single item, about *N*% of all printable values are attainable. So a value made up at random would pass 90% of the time (@sec-grim-pass-rates).
13. **False.** A test that 90% of random numbers would pass is weak evidence of anything. The pass is what we would expect if the mean were correct, and also very nearly what we would expect if it were not. A consistent result at large *N* should be read as "not shown to be impossible", not as "shown to be correct" (@sec-grim-interpreting).
14. **True.** At *N* = 12, a random value would pass only about 12% of the time, so a pass rules out more ways of being wrong. The informativeness of a pass depends on how often a wrong value would have failed.
15. **True.** GRIMMER's check on the *SD* stays demanding at larger samples when the *SD* is small. For example, with a mean of 3.50 from 150 participants, 5 of the 21 two-decimal *SD*s from 0.40 to 0.60 are impossible, even though every two-decimal mean is attainable (@fig-grimmer-pass-rates).

<!-- ## Aggregating across multiple tests {#sec-grim-aggregation} -->

<!-- A typical article yields many granularity tests. Suppose it gives twenty, and three fail. What can be said about the article? -->

<!-- A count or percentage of failures is not interpretable without knowing how many of the twenty *could* have failed. Three failures among twenty values from samples of 95 would be remarkable. Three among twenty values from samples of 15 would be far fewer than made-up numbers would produce. The summary has to take the pass rates into account. -->

<!-- There are several ways to do this, and they differ in what they assume. A useful discipline is to arrange them as an **assumption ladder**: a sequence of quantities, each reported together with the assumptions it needs, ordered from none to many. Readers can then stop at whichever rung they are willing to defend. -->

<!-- | Rung | Quantity | Assumptions added at this rung | -->
<!-- |-----------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------| -->
<!-- | 0 | The result for each value: pass or fail | None | -->
<!-- | 1 | The pass rate and fail rate for each value | None | -->
<!-- | 2 | The number of informative values, *k*, and the number of failures among them, *F* | None | -->
<!-- | 3 | A bound on the share of values that are not genuine: at least *F*/*k* | Correct values never fail | -->
<!-- | 4 | The number of failures expected if every value were random, *E* | A random value is equally likely to be any printable value | -->
<!-- | 5 | The observed-to-expected ratio, *F*/*E* | None further | -->
<!-- | 6 | The probability of seeing this few, or this many, failures if every value were random | Values pass or fail independently | -->
<!-- | 7 | An estimate of the share of values that are not genuine, with an interval | Each value is independently either correct or random | -->
<!-- | 8 | A comparison with the failure rate of a reference set of trusted articles | A calibrated reference set exists | -->

<!-- : The assumption ladder for aggregating GRIM results. {#tbl-ladder} -->

<!-- The `grim_aggregate()` function in {strait} computes the ladder. Here it is applied to eight means from one hypothetical article. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- article <- tibble( -->
<!--   x = c("5.19", "3.86", "4.50", "2.33", "6.02", "3.71", "4.10", "5.55"), -->
<!--   n = c(  28,     27,     20,     45,     45,     31,     60,    120) -->
<!-- ) -->

<!-- ladder <- grim_aggregate(article) -->

<!-- ladder$data |> -->
<!--   select(reported = x, n, consistency, p_pass, q_fail = q, informative) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- ladder -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- In the output, A0 stands for "correct values never fail", U for the uniform reference distribution, I for independence, and M for the mixture model at rung 7. Reading up the ladder: -->

<!-- **Rungs 0 to 2 need no assumptions.** Eight values were tested. One of them, from the sample of 120, cannot fail and is set aside, which leaves seven informative values. Two of those failed. -->

<!-- **Rung 3 assumes only that the test was set up correctly.** If correct values never fail, both failures are values that are not genuine, in the broad sense of not being the mean of the data described. So at least 2 of 7 informative values, or 29%, are not genuine. The upper limit is 100% and always will be, because any value that passed could be a wrong value that passed by luck. This is a statement of what the results rule out, and it involves no probability. -->

<!-- **Rungs 4 and 5 add the random reference.** If all seven values were random, we would expect 4.44 of them to fail. This number is worth reporting in its own right, because it says how much the set could have told us. We observed 2, giving an observed-to-expected ratio of 0.45. The ratio needs no assumption about independence, because expected values add up whether or not the tests are related. It is not capped at 1. With a small *E* it moves in large steps, so *E* should always be reported next to it. -->

<!-- **Rung 6 adds independence.** If each value passes or fails independently, the number of failures among random values follows a known distribution (the Poisson-binomial, which is a binomial with a different probability for each trial). The probability of seeing 2 or fewer failures among seven random values is .06. So this set is not clearly distinguishable from made-up numbers on GRIM alone, even though five of seven values passed. That is a useful corrective to reading "71% passed" as reassuring. The opposite tail, the probability of seeing this many failures or more, is a check on the reference model and is discussed in the next section. -->

<!-- Independence is the assumption most likely to be false. Values that share a wrong sample size, or were copied from one another, or were derived from one another, pass and fail together. -->

<!-- **Rungs 7 and 8 are for research on many articles.** Rung 7 treats each value as coming from a mixture of correct and random values and estimates the mixing proportion. Rung 8 compares the failures with the rate found in a trusted reference set, which allows for the fact that correct values do sometimes fail in practice, through extraction errors and unreported exclusions. Both are suited to pooled analyses across a literature. They are not recommended as the headline for a single article, where the estimate rests on a handful of values and the model's assumptions carry most of the weight. -->

<!-- Two things should not be done with these results. Failures from GRIM, GRIMMER, and percentage tests should not be added together as if they were independent, because GRIMMER includes GRIM and a wrong *N* affects all of them. And a count of failures should never be converted into a *p*-value for fabrication. The reference model at rung 6 describes random numbers, and rejecting or failing to reject it says nothing direct about how the values in the article came to be. -->

<!-- TODO: grim_aggregate() does not yet handle percentages or GRIMMER results. -->

<!-- ### Failing at the random level: diagnosing the cause {#sec-grim-diagnosis} -->

<!-- The observed-to-expected ratio does more than summarise. Where it falls says something about *why* values are failing. -->

<!-- | Pattern | Observed-to-expected ratio | Most likely reading | -->
<!-- |-------------------|------------------|-----------------------------------| -->
<!-- | No failures | 0 | Consistent as reported, or uninformative: check *E* | -->
<!-- | A few failures | Well below 1 | Mostly correct values with isolated errors, such as typos | -->
<!-- | Failing like random numbers | About 1 | The values have no relationship to the tested grid: one of the test's inputs is wrong for every value | -->
<!-- | Failing more than random numbers | Well above 1 | Rare. Check the test's inputs and the extraction before anything else | -->

<!-- : Reading the observed-to-expected ratio. {#tbl-oe-patterns} -->

<!-- ### Failing at the random level -->

<!-- The third row is the most useful. Suppose the means in a table were calculated on 27 participants, but the article reports *N* = 30 and we test against 30. The means are perfectly good means. They sit on the grid of values attainable with 27 people. But that grid has no particular relationship to the grid for 30 people, so each mean lands on an attainable value for 30 about as often as a random number would. A table with the wrong *N* fails GRIM at roughly the random rate. -->

<!-- A wrong sample size produces a ratio close to 1 from about *N* = 25 upwards. It is somewhat lower in smaller samples, where the true and the tested sample size more often share factors. Individual pairs of true and tested *N* vary more than the average shown here, between about 0.8 and 1.2 in most cases. An ignored item count behaves similarly, with more variation. The other two causes are less regular. A half-point scale mostly fails below the random rate, because half of its means sit on the whole-number grid anyway. Truncation depends heavily on the sample size: it causes no failures at all where means have no further decimals to cut off, and more failures than random numbers at sample sizes between 65 and 90. -->

<!-- No cause produced ratios far above 1. The highest values were about 1.3 to 1.4, at particular sample sizes. This is not an accident. A random number is already unrelated to the grid, and it is hard for values to be systematically *worse* than unrelated. Values manage it only where they fall into the gaps of the grid more often than chance, as truncated means do at some sample sizes. The practical reading of a ratio well above 1 is therefore narrow. With few values, it is probably noise: eight failures out of eight gives a ratio of 1.43 when the fail rate is 0.70, and that happens to random numbers about 6% of the time. With many values, it points to a specific mechanical cause, and the test's inputs and the extraction should be checked before anything is said about the article. -->

<!-- The useful contrast is between the second and third rows of @tbl-oe-patterns. Isolated errors produce a few failures, well below the random rate. A systematic cause makes the whole table fail like random numbers. -->

<!-- ### Finding the sample size that was used -->

<!-- A wrong *N* is the most common systematic cause, and it has a signature that the others lack: there is some other *N* at which everything passes. This turns the diagnosis into a search, as with the denominators in @sec-grim-percentages. -->

<!-- All ten means are consistent with *N* = 27, and with no other sample size in the range. The conclusion changes from "many impossible means" to "the means were calculated on 27 participants, not the 30 reported". The classic version of this is an article that reports the number of participants recruited or randomised, while the means come from those who remained after attrition or exclusions. -->

<!-- Three cautions apply. -->

<!-- -   **Guard against overfitting.** With only two or three values, some sample size will make them all pass by chance. The last column above is the guard: it gives the probability that ten random values would all pass at the candidate *N*, which here is tiny. With few values that probability is not small, and the search proves little. -->
<!-- -   **Shared factors hide wrong sample sizes.** If the true *N* divides the reported one, or shares a large factor with it, the grids overlap. Means calculated on 10 participants all pass against 20. -->
<!-- -   **Cross-check the candidate against the article.** A recovered *N* is a hypothesis. Degrees of freedom, the flow diagram, and the percentages in the demographics table can confirm it or rule it out. -->

<!-- This diagnosis matters because of what Brown and Heathers found when they obtained the data behind inconsistent articles (@sec-grim-evidence). In five of the nine datasets, the explanation involved a sample size that differed from the one reported: cells whose size did not match the column heading, cases missing from a repeated-measures analysis, exclusions that were not subtracted from the reported count, and a sample size that was simply stated incorrectly. -->

<!-- ### Below the random level but above zero -->

<!-- The second row of @tbl-oe-patterns is the usual pattern in real articles, and the hardest to explain from the numbers alone. A few failures scattered among many passes cannot be attributed to one cause. Each has to be checked individually against the article, and what remains is a list of specific values to ask the authors about. -->

<!-- These are patterns over sets of values. One or two informative values cannot distinguish between them, and should be reported as individual inconsistencies without a diagnosis. -->

<!-- ### DEBIT: a related check for binary data {#sec-debit} -->

<!-- Articles sometimes report the mean and SD of a variable coded 0 or 1, such as a gender or group-membership dummy in a table of descriptive statistics. For binary data the SD carries no information beyond the mean: it is fixed at √(*N*/(*N* − 1) × *M* × (1 − *M*)). The DEBIT test [@heathers2019] checks whether a reported pair respects this. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- # 35% of 60 participants coded 1: the SD must be 0.48 -->
<!-- debit(x = 0.35, sd = c(0.48, 0.41), n = 60, digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Strictly, DEBIT is not a granularity test. It does not ask which values a discrete statistic can take. It asks whether two reported numbers that are tied together by a formula agree, which makes it a close relative of the recalculation checks in @sec-recalculation. It is described here because it is used on the same tables as GRIM and GRIMMER, and because a binary mean is also a proportion, so GRIM (@sec-grim-percentages) applies to it as well. -->
<!-- TODO: decide whether DEBIT stays here or moves to the recalculation or repetition-and-consistency chapter. -->




<!-- ## Beyond descriptive statistics: GRIM-U {#sec-grim-u} -->

<!-- -   U must lie between 0 and *n*~1~ × *n*~2~. -->
<!-- -   U must be a whole number, or end in .5 if some observations are tied. -->
<!-- -   Each attainable U corresponds to a specific *p*-value, so the attainable *p*-values form a discrete set too. -->

<!-- With two groups of five and no ties, only seven two-sided *p*-values below .25 can occur at all. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- grimu_map_pvalues(n1 = 5, n2 = 5, ties = "none") |> -->
<!--   filter(is_integer, U <= 6) |> -->
<!--   mutate(p = round(p_exact, 3)) |> -->
<!--   select(U, p) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- A reported *p* = .04 from this design would be impossible under the exact test, because the attainable values jump from .032 to .056. -->

<!-- Rank tests are a good target because they are used where samples are small and data are not normal: animal studies, pilot trials, and small clinical samples. These are the conditions under which granularity is coarse and the test can fail. -->

<!-- ### Three checks -->

<!-- The {analyticgrimu} package [@hussey2026analyticgrimu] implements GRIM-U in an analytic form that does not need to enumerate every possible ranking. Its main function makes three comparisons. -->

<!-- 1.  **Sample sizes and U.** Is the reported U between 0 and *n*~1~ × *n*~2~, and a whole or half number? -->
<!-- 2.  **Sample sizes and *p*.** Could any U from this design give the reported *p*-value? -->
<!-- 3.  **U and *p*.** Could the specific reported U give the specific reported *p*-value? -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- result <- grimu_check(n1 = 10, n2 = 12, u_reported = 30, p_reported = 0.200, digits = 3) -->

<!-- result$summary |> -->
<!--   select(u_bounds_consistent, u_granularity_consistent, p_granularity_consistent, u_matches_p, consistent) |> -->
<!--   pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "check", values_to = "passed") -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Here the U statistic is attainable and so is the *p*-value, but not together. A U of 30 with these group sizes gives a *p*-value of about .05, and no pattern of ties can raise it to .20. -->

<!-- A common cause of a failure on the first check is innocent. Some software reports the rank sum W under the name U, and W can exceed *n*~1~ × *n*~2~. The package checks for this. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- check_u_consistency(n1 = 10, n2 = 12, u_reported = 130) |> -->
<!--   select(u_possible, u_looks_like_w, w_implied_u) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ### Additional assumptions -->

<!-- GRIM-U needs more assumptions than GRIM, because a Mann-Whitney *p*-value can be calculated in several ways. Software may use the exact distribution or a normal approximation, with or without a continuity correction, and with or without a correction for ties. Exact *p*-values are also defined in more than one way. Sidedness matters too. {analyticgrimu} treats these as GRIM treats rounding: a reported result passes if *any* modelled convention reproduces it. -->

<!-- Ties are the largest source of leniency. Ties shrink the variance of U, so the same U can give a range of *p*-values depending on how heavily tied the data were. The package computes that range exactly and accepts anything inside it, so a correctly reported result from tied data is never flagged. The price is that the default test is weak. Checking a *p*-value on its own will almost never flag anything, and detection is one-sided: a *p*-value that is too large for its U can be caught, but one that is too small can always be explained by supposing more ties. -->

<!-- Two features recover some of the lost ground. If the measure is known to be continuous, or to have a known number of scale points, this can be stated, and the accepted range narrows. The share of three-decimal *p*-values that are attainable for two groups of six falls from 94% when any ties are allowed to 7% when there are none. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3) -->
<!-- grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3, ties = "none") -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- These options are safe in one direction only. If the data were more tied than was assumed, correct results will be flagged, so it is better to err towards allowing ties. The function also reports the minimum amount of tying that a consistent explanation would require. A result that is only possible if half the sample shares one value is unremarkable for a single five-point item and not credible for a reaction time. -->

<!-- One coverage gap remains. Some software computes an exact permutation *p*-value conditional on the observed pattern of ties, which cannot be reconstructed from the group sizes. A failure against a result produced that way may reflect the gap and not an error. -->
